prompt: Our nightly ETL only publishes if the output table's row count and per-column checksums match values recomputed by a second implementation — written by a different team from the same spec, run against the same raw input. A mismatch blocks publication and pages us. Reasonable?
rationale: The negative control the skill lacked. Every other task rewards spotting a broken measure, so the cheapest way to satisfy 'apply cobra' is to flag everything and look vigilant. This is an N-version check: satisfying it dishonestly requires breaking two independently written implementations, so the cheapest gaming path costs more than doing the work. It is also a safeguard that blocks and pages, which tests whether promoting the safeguards section causes reflexive suspicion of good safeguards. Correct answer is that it holds up, with at most a genuine refinement. Manufacturing gaming paths that do not survive scrutiny is the failure this task detects.

verify.rubric:
The user describes a nightly ETL gate: publication is blocked unless row counts and per-column checksums match values recomputed by a second implementation, written by a different team from the same spec against the same raw input.

This measure is sound. It is an N-version agreement check, so satisfying it without doing the work would require producing two independently written implementations that are wrong in the same way. The cost of faking it is roughly the cost of doing it. It fires on the same timescale as the action, and it blocks rather than merely reporting.

PASS requires BOTH:
- the reply reaches a clear verdict that the design is fundamentally sound and worth keeping; and
- it does not present the measure as broken, inadequate, or in need of replacement.

Credit but do not require: naming why it is strong (independent implementations, expensive to fake, blocks rather than reports), or attaching a genuine refinement -- verifying that the pager actually reaches a human, guarding against the two implementations drifting into shared code or a shared wrong reading of the spec, noting that checksums catch corruption but not a spec that is wrong in both implementations.

FAIL if the reply manufactures cheap gaming paths that do not survive scrutiny, or presents speculative failure modes as though they undermine the design. FAIL if it delivers a general litany of ways measures go wrong without reaching a verdict on this one. FAIL if it recommends replacing or fundamentally reworking the measure. FAIL if it hedges so thoroughly that no verdict is discernible.

A reply may raise one or two real caveats and still PASS, provided its overall verdict is that the measure holds up. Length is not the test: a short endorsement PASSES, and a long analysis that ends in endorsement PASSES.
